https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/03/csep.text: Menü Kereső Hogyan lehetséges ez? – Kátai-Németh Vilmos nekiment a csepeli polgármesternek, az önkormányzat válaszolt Belföld Joób Sándor Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom „Amikor olyan alacsony a Duna vízállása, hogy le kell állítani a paksi atomerőművet, aközben Csepelen mennek a szökőkutak, ég a díszkivilágítás, locsolják a focipályákat, közparkokat, és az emberek azt kérdezik tőlem: hogyan lehetséges ez. Én is ezt kérdezem Borbély Lénárd polgármestertől, hogy hogyan lehetséges ez” – ezekkel a szavakkal ment neki egy Facebook-videóban a városrész exfideszes polgármesterének Kátai-Németh Vilmos szociális és családügyi miniszter, aki Csepel országgyűlési képviselője is. Kátai-Németh szerint egy országos vízügyi és energetikai válság közepén egy városvezetőnek érzékelnie kell a problémát és megtenni a szükséges lépéseket. Felszólította ezért Borbélyt, hogy hozzon víz- és energiatakarékossági intézkedéseket, ha pedig ezt nem tudja vagy nem akarja megtenni, akkor vállalja a politikai felelősséget. Borbély Lénárdot a Németh Szilárddal való konfliktusa miatt 2023-ban kizáratták a Fideszből, de függetlenként 2024-ben 67 százalékos eredménnyel választották újra Csepel polgármesterévé, miközben a Fidesz jelöltje csupán 10 százalékot kapott. Kátai-Németh felszólítása után megkerestük a csepeli önkormányzatot, ahonnan részletes választ küldtek arról, hogyan kezelték eddig a helyzetet és mit terveznek. Az önkormányzat azt írta: a rendkívüli energia- és vízellátási helyzet kezdete óta folyamatosan hoznak intézkedéseket, hogy a kerületben a közszolgáltatások működése és a lakosság ellátása biztonságosan fenntartható legyen. Már a múlt héten megkezdték a felkészülést, és az első szükséges intézkedéseket akkor meghozták. A mostani korlátozások nem egyetlen nap alatt, hanem egy előre megkezdett, folyamatosan bővülő intézkedéssorozat részeként léptek életbe. A múlt héten felállt az önkormányzat operatív stábja, amely a közigazgatási szünet idején is naponta értékeli a helyzetet, figyelemmel kíséri az országos döntéseket és szükség esetén további helyi intézkedésekről dönt; a bölcsődék, óvodák, egészségügyi és szociális intézmények, valamint az idősellátás folyamatosan működnek, az intézmények klimatizáltak; ideiglenesen szünetel az önkormányzati sportpályák és a strand világítása; átmenetileg bezártak a közművelődési intézmények; leálltak az önkormányzati szökőkutak; ivóvízzel nem locsolnak, a párakapuk sem üzemelnek, a fiatal fákat és a kiemelt jelentőségű zöldfelületeket kizárólag saját fúrt kutak vizének felhasználásával, vagyis ivóvíz felhasználása nélkül öntözik; az önkormányzat minden intézményében és gazdasági társaságánál energiatakarékossági intézkedéseket vezettek be; az önkormányzati világításokat lekapcsolták, az Ady Endre Családsegítő Közösségi Ház ideiglenesen bezárt, a Csepeli Piac pedig módosított nyitvatartás szerint működik. Emellett megkezdték a felkészülést arra is, hogy szükség esetén további intézkedéseket vezessenek be. A héten több helyszínen ingyenes ivóvízosztást szerveznek, kiemelt figyelmet fordítanak az egyedül élő idősekre, a segítségre szorulókra és a hajléktalan emberekre. A rendkívüli hőségre tekintettel a Csepeli Strandfürdő nyitvatartását is meghosszabbították. „Folyamatosan figyelemmel kísérjük a helyzet alakulását, és amennyiben azt a körülmények indokolják, készek vagyunk további lépések megtételére is” – írták. Photograph: Brian Snyder/Reuters View image in fullscreen A Flock Safety camera mounted on a pole beneath a solar panel in Waltham, Massachusetts, on 24 August 2026. Photograph: Brian Snyder/Reuters Technology Analysis Cut the cameras: Flock surveillance cameras spur rare bipartisan backlash Thor Benson Politicians on the right and left are pushing back against Flock as more Americans voice opposition to the tech Sat 5 Sep 2026 10.00 EDT Share Growing factions from both sides of the political aisle in the US are pushing back against surveillance cameras made by a single company, a rare response in a sharply divided country with a president pushing an unwaveringly pro-tech agenda. The bipartisan backlash against Flock Safety cameras resembles nationwide rage toward the construction of large datacenters that power artificial intelligence. Polling shows roughly 75% of Americans oppose new datacenter construction in their areas. Flock’s cameras are automated license plate readers (ALPRs), which take pictures of vehicle license plates so police and security companies can log the movement of cars in a given area. There are about 120,000 Flock cameras across the US, which conduct roughly 2bn scans per month. The company is staring down controversy after reports of abuses of its cameras by police officers in multiple states, who have used them to stalk ex-lovers and track people seeking abortions. The network the cameras feed into is also frequently utilized by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Data and polling from the Washington Post show that social media posts about Flock have increased since July, and about 46% of Americans oppose ALPRs being used in their community – up 13 points from the previous year. Vigilantes are posting videos of themselves destroying the cameras to digital applause. According to privacy and surveillance experts, hatred of Flock cameras has become bipartisan. “In my 20-plus years at the ACLU, I’ve never really seen such a grassroots uprising against surveillance technology like this,” said Jay Stanley, a senior policy analyst at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). “On the left, there’s a historical memory of law enforcement spying on and interfering with advocates for social change … On the right, there’s a long tradition of ‘don’t tread on me’ – keep the government out of my life, keep it from looking over my shoulder.” Both liberal and conservative politicians are pushing back against Flock cameras. Greg Abbott, Texas’s Republican governor, blocked state agencies from procuring Flock products. On the other side of the political spectrum, Bernie Sanders, the progressive US senator, is promising to introduce legislation to restrict the use of Flock cameras. Republican senator Josh Hawley has launched an investigation into potential Flock privacy abuses, and Democratic congressman Ro Khanna is cosponsoring a bill with Republican congressman Thomas Massie to prevent federal funds from being used to purchase Flock cameras. Municipal leaders of all political stripes are dropping contracts with Flock , though sometimes they replace the license plate readers with another brand of camera and continue the surveillance. We reached out to Flock Safety for a statement and did not receive a response before publishing. Surveillance hasn’t always been a unifying topic in US politics. Debates over the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (Fisa), the Patriot Act and other surveillance issues have often been divisive. This appears to be an unusual case where politicians are getting on the same side of a hot-button issue. “Privacy, to some extent, is bipartisan,” said Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. “When you put up these cameras, they last longer than the current administration. You might trust the people in power now who put them up – but are you going to trust the next people who get access to that equipment?” Americans have been showing up at town hall meetings by the dozen over the past six months or so, and there have been numerous protests to show opposition to Flock surveillance cameras around the country. More than 100 jurisdictions have canceled their contracts so far, according to data from the non-profit Institute for Justice. An organization called DeFlock, founded in 2024, hopes to increase the numbers by compiling a map of the cameras’ locations. While ALPRs aren’t new, Flock, founded in 2017, has made them far more prevalent than they used to be. The company’s software allows disparate law enforcement agencies to share data with one another, meaning a license plate scan by a police department in one state could easily and quickly be used in another. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to TechScape A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives after newsletter promotion “Flock represents tech companies in bed with governments, doing the exact stuff people have become distrustful of and resentful about for the past few decades. It feels like it’s finally hit the boiling-over point,” said Woodrow Hartzog, a professor of law and computer science at Boston University. Hartzog predicts the actions against Flock Safety will continue at the state and local level amid this growing popular outrage. He expects people are going to stay angry about the issue, and politicians will have to respond. “The pushback we’re seeing against Flock cameras is one of the most vivid illustrations I can think of that surveillance is not inevitable – that these tools aren’t inevitable,” Hartzog says. “It’s up to all of us to stop them.” Explore more on these topics Technology Surveillance Democrats Republicans US politics Datacenters – US Privacy analysis Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK US politics World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine Football Newsletters Business Environment UK politics Science Tech Global development Obituaries

(Ukrainian Emergency Service via AP) (Ukrainian Emergency Service/AP via AP) By SAMYA KULLAB, Associated Press October 06, 2026 at 11:13 am EDT KYIV, Ukraine — Russian air defenses intercepted nearly 900 Ukrainian drones overnight over multiple regions of the country, as well as the occupied Crimean Peninsula and the Sea of Azov, the Defense Ministry in Moscow said Tuesday. Unconfirmed media reports said a major fuel depot in the Moscow region was on fire after the attack that killed two people. Ukraine's domestically developed long-range drones and, increasingly, missiles have allowed Kyiv to hit Russian soil during the more than 4 ½ years since Moscow's forces launched a full-scale invasion . It has hit targets as far east as the Urals and Siberia. The bigger Russian military's air superiority during the war has made aerial attacks on civilian areas of Ukraine routine. Ukrainian officials are now bracing for what President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Tuesday is an upcoming “massive” aerial attack by Russia. “Today, we received updated intelligence on Russia’s preparations for a massive strike. We are preparing countermeasures,” Zelenskyy said on social media. “We set deadlines for a significant part of the tasks, and the highest-priority ones are already being implemented.” Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said last week that Kyiv estimates Russia is holding 600 ballistic missiles in reserve and can produce up to 140 ballistic missiles per month. Without ammunition for its U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems , which is in short supply, Ukraine is at the mercy of Russia's ballistic weapons. Ukraine fires more than 700 drones toward the Moscow region Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 650 drones flew toward the capital region between Monday evening and Tuesday morning. Most were destroyed far away, and 105 were downed as they approached the city, he said. Sobyanin later reported 68 more drones targeting Moscow were downed during daylight on Tuesday morning. Ukraine has regularly targeted Russian oil refineries and storage depots, claiming last weekend that it had disabled 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity. The claim could not be independently verified. Russian President Vladimir Putin said last week that the attacks had cost Russia roughly 1% of its gross domestic product. Russia has traditionally been the world's third-largest producer of refined fuel products from crude oil, after the U.S. and China. The Kremlin has banned diesel exports due to the Ukrainian strikes, pushing global prices higher. That prompted U.S. President Donald Trump last month to urge Ukraine to stop hitting Russia's refineries. After hitting Kyiv bridges, Russia targets a bridge in southern Ukraine After several days of targeting bridges in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv, as part of a campaign to make civilian life difficult, Russia attacked one of the bridges over the Dnipro River in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia, according to Mykhailo Semikin, the regional military administration chief. Traffic across the bridge was temporarily suspended, he said. A nighttime Russian attack on a Zaporizhzhia residential building wounded five people and a daylight strike on a warehouse in the city caused a large fire, Semikin said. Russian forces are also trying to choke shipping in Ukrainian ports in the Black Sea, denying Kyiv vital grain export revenue . The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces overnight struck targets in Ukraine's southern Odesa region on the Black Sea coast with drones. An ammunition depot was hit, as were a bulk carrier in the Chornomorsk port carrying dual-use goods and port infrastructure in Izmail, the ministry said. A Russian drone strike in the Black Sea hit a cargo ship flying the flag of the Marshall Islands, killing one person and wounding seven others, Odesa regional governor Oleh Kiper said. The vessel was carrying rapeseed oil, he said. Moscow warns against a bigger US presence in Lithuania A senior Russian official criticized developments in Lithuania, saying they would escalate tensions in the region. The Baltic nation has offered to host a U.S. military base and the Lithuanian parliament is voting on a bill to allow the deployment of American nuclear weapons. “If military infrastructure belonging to a key NATO member moves closer to our borders, then naturally, this can only be perceived as a step toward escalating tensions, just like the deployment of nuclear weapons on the territory of a neighboring state,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters. Trump said Monday he would consider establishing a permanent U.S. military base in Lithuania, one of three small Baltic states seen as particularly vulnerable to Russia. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned last month that Moscow is planning hybrid strikes with drones or rockets on European countries supporting Ukraine, which include Poland and Lithuania. Meanwhile, Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said Tuesday his country will deploy Patriot air-defense systems and about 100 troops to Poland to help protect the airport in Rzeszow, which is the main logistics hub for military aid deliveries to Ukraine. ___ AP reporter Claudia Ciobanu in Warsaw, Poland contributed to this story. ___ Follow the AP's coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine Copyright 2026 The Associated Press.
